answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Jonathan Swift wrote it in a letter to Henry St John, Lord Bolingbroke, dated 5 April 1729, telling him he had made a maxim “that a wise man ought to have money in his head, but not in his heart.” The letter is printed in The Works of the Rev. Jonathan Swift, Vol. 14 and in the 1808 Works (ed. Sheridan & Nichols) at p.380. Modern quotation clips his “ought to have” to “should have.”

source.excerpt: … I have made a maxim, that should be writ in letters of diamonds, that a wise man ought to have money in his head, but not in his heart.
trail: The line is absent from Wikiquote’s Jonathan Swift page — it appears in neither the sourced, disputed, nor misattributed sections.
It does not appear in Swift’s aphorism collection Thoughts on Various Subjects, whose genuine money maxims are worded quite differently.
Quote-aggregator sites such as BrainyQuote and Due present it as Swift’s with no citation whatsoever.

author.name: Jonathan Swift
author.heading: Who wrote it
author.bio: Jonathan Swift was the Dublin-born Dean of St Patrick’s Cathedral and the age’s greatest prose satirist, author of Gulliver’s Travels, A Modest Proposal and A Tale of a Tub. He did write pointed aphorisms about money — his Thoughts on Various Subjects includes lines such as “No man will take counsel, but every man will take money.” This head-versus-heart maxim is one more of them — written not in an essay but in a 1729 letter to his friend Lord Bolingbroke.

misattribution.heading: Genuinely Swift — with one word clipped
misattribution.intro: The attribution is correct: Swift really did write this, in a 1729 letter to Lord Bolingbroke. The only thing worth flagging is the wording — the version everyone shares quietly clips his “ought to have” down to “should have.”

items.why: Swift wrote “a wise man ought to have money in his head, but not in his heart” in his 5 April 1729 letter to Lord Bolingbroke. The version in circulation clips “ought to have” to “should have” — the sense is unchanged, but it is not quite his words.

Swift’s letter to Bolingbroke is genuine and documented. The further flourish — that Bolingbroke wrote back a matching reply about money reaching the heart — circulates in unsourced restatements and cannot be confirmed from the primary correspondence; treat that part with caution.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest verdict: Swift really did write this — in his 5 April 1729 letter to Lord Bolingbroke — and modern quotation simply clips his “ought to have” to “should have.”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Swift is one of the internet’s biggest quote magnets, so plenty of money maxims get pinned on him with no basis. This one is different: it really is his, tucked into a 1729 letter to his friend Lord Bolingbroke rather than any published essay.

The head-versus-heart framing (be shrewd about money, don’t let it rule you) reads like modern personal-finance advice, which is part of why people assume it must be a later invention. It isn’t — Swift wrote “ought to have money in his head, but not in his heart,” and the familiar “should have” is just a clipped retelling.
context.pull: His own words — from a 1729 letter, lightly clipped.
